title: Sparks of Weight-Space Programming for Robot Foundation Models
abstract: This paper demonstrates an approach for correcting failures of robot foundation models (RFMs) without additional data collection, demonstrations, or training. We apply weight-space programming (WSP), in which a language-model agent directly reads and writes a neural network's parameters, to a large, pre-trained vision-language-action policy. The idea is simple: many policy failures are not random but repeatedly land in the same recognizable stuck state, so if that state is visible in the model's internal activations, a small edit could trigger a corrective movement while leaving the rest of the model's parameters unchanged. A core design choice is where to write the edit: repurposing a few near-silent neurons in the action expert lets the edit switch on in situations associated with the failure and produce a corrective movement, such as lowering the gripper toward the target, that is specified directly rather than learned through training. Empirically, when applied to the pi0.5 policy in simulation, we find that edits to roughly 0.0002% of the parameters can improve success on recurring failures, including for a policy that was already fine-tuned on its task. Reversed and random edits indicate that the gains come from the intended behavior, and the approach works best when the failure situation is recognizable and a simple correction can address it.

affiliation_source_text: Weight-Space Programming for Targeted Repair of Robot Foundation Models Kyle Coelho, Eugen Solowjow Siemens Research kyle.coelho@siemens.com Introduction Weight-space programming (WSP) asks whether a language -model agent can inspect and directly write a neural network’s parameters, instead of adapting it through gradient descent. MIT’s initial WSP report [1] brought this idea into view, showing that frontier LLMs such as GPT Astra can directly read, edit, and write the weights of neural networks to achieve a desired behavior and end goal. This was showcased on vision tasks and math problem solving, among others. Within two weeks of the authors’ post, the results attracted considerable attention due to the potentially profound implications of WSP. We report the application of WSP to robot foundation models (RFMs) and show how failure modes of an RFM can be mitigated without additional data collection or training. We test whether failures of RFM policies can be corrected through direct weight editing. Our hypothesis is that many failures are not random: the policy repeatedly lands in the same recognizable stuck state, such as hovering above a target or being unable to reach a target pose. If that situation is recognizable in the model’s internal activations, a small edit can use that signal to trigger a correction while leaving the other model parameters unchanged. Prior work has directly edited robot policies in weight space. Stranghöner et al. wrote state-dependent controllers into unused units of behavior-cloning policies [2].
